common_name: Blue Glow Agave (Compact Hybrid Agave with Glowing Leaf Margins)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; Blue Glow is a compact hybrid agave that stays smaller and better-behaved than Agave americana, without the sharp terminal spines of many agave species.

directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; agave requires perfect drainage and will rot quickly in heavy clay or wet sites. Blue Glow is a hybrid agave prized for its compact, symmetrical rosette of smooth, blue-green leaves edged in a thin, glowing gold-and-red margin that appears almost illuminated when backlit by low sun, an effect that has made it one of the most popular ornamental agave hybrids for modern xeric and container design. Unlike many agave species it lacks the vicious terminal spine, making it safer to site near paths and seating areas. It needs essentially no supplemental water once established beyond occasional deep soaking during extended drought, and its smaller mature size fits containers and smaller garden beds better than large agave species.

common_name: Color Guard Yucca (Variegated Gold-Striped Adam's Needle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Color Guard is a variegated selection of native Adam's needle yucca, with a bold central gold stripe on each leaf that provides year-round color even without flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Color Guard is a striking variegated form of the native Adam's needle yucca, with each sword-shaped, evergreen leaf marked by a broad creamy-yellow central stripe bordered in blue-green, giving strong architectural color to the garden year-round rather than only during its tall summer flower spike of white bell-shaped blooms. Like the species it is extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable to poor soils once established, needing almost no supplemental care. It slowly produces offsets (pups) at the base that can be separated to propagate new plants, and spent flower stalks can be cut down after bloom.

common_name: Angelina Sedum (Glowing Gold Needle-Leaf Groundcover Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Angelina spreads quickly into a dense, low mat and roots readily from broken stem pieces, making it easy to propagate and fill in bare, dry, sunny spots.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun. Angelina is one of the most widely planted groundcover sedums, forming a dense, low, spreading mat of needle-like, bright chartreuse-gold foliage that takes on warm orange-red tones in cold weather, giving strong seasonal color change in a low-maintenance planting. It spreads quickly by rooting along its trailing stems, making it useful for covering dry slopes, edging pathways, spilling over retaining walls, or filling gaps between pavers, and broken stem pieces root readily wherever they touch soil. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and needs essentially no supplemental care beyond occasional trimming to keep it within bounds.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Dragon's Blood spreads into a dense, low mat with deep burgundy-red summer foliage tones and clusters of small star-shaped red flowers in mid-to-late summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun. Dragon's Blood is a classic groundcover sedum forming a dense, spreading mat of rounded, fleshy leaves that deepen to rich burgundy-red in full sun and cooler weather, topped in mid-to-late summer with clusters of small, star-shaped, deep red flowers that draw butterflies and bees. It spreads readily by rooting along creeping stems, making it a reliable, low-maintenance groundcover for dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and the edges of paths, and it tolerates poor, lean soil and drought far better than most groundcovers. It needs almost no care beyond an occasional trim to control spread into neighboring plantings.

common_name: Santa Rita Prickly Pear (Purple-Padded Ornamental Cactus)

planting.note: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy or rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; Santa Rita's signature purple pad color intensifies in cold, dry weather and with stress from drought or poor soil, while it stays greener in richer, wetter conditions.

directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun. Santa Rita prickly pear is grown chiefly for its striking blue-gray pads that flush a deep violet-purple in cold or drought stress, providing dramatic color contrast in a xeric or desert-style planting alongside its cheerful yellow spring flowers and edible purple fruit (tunas) later in the season. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established, needing essentially no supplemental water, and propagates easily from rooted pad cuttings allowed to callus for a few days before planting. Handle with heavy gloves, since the pads carry both larger spines and fine, irritating glochids that detach easily on contact.
